editorial.headline: Porcelain Construction Wholesale: Open Nationally, Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This wholesale activity spans porcelain toilets, basins, baths and wall tiles—open to full foreign ownership nationally, but unavailable to PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
For a foreign investor considering this activity in Bali, the decisive fact is straightforward: it cannot be registered there as a PMA business today. That is not because the national position is closed. Nationally, the activity is open to foreign investment, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. Bali applies an island-wide, permanent bar on PMA for KBLI activities assessed at Low or Medium-Low risk. For this activity, OSS places every scope at Low or Medium-Low risk at the Large scale, so the Bali moratorium blocks the registration.

The activity itself is wholesale trade in porcelain construction materials. Its practical subject matter is clearly defined: porcelain toilets, bidets, washbasins, urinals, sinks, bathtubs and wall tiles. The code is therefore about the wholesale dealing of these construction-related porcelain products, not a broad catch-all for construction activity. That specificity matters when reading the national openness alongside Bali’s restriction: the assessment attaches to this stated activity and its scopes.

Registration is open across the full business-size range listed for the activity: Micro, Small, Medium and Large. The Bali issue arises at the Large scale, where every scope is assessed as Low or Medium-Low risk. Under the provincial moratorium, that risk outcome is enough to prevent PMA registration. The restriction is not described as a partial local cap on foreign ownership; it is a block on PMA registration for this activity in Bali.

That produces a clean but important distinction. At the national level, foreign investment is permitted up to 100%, so there is no national foreign-ownership cap below full ownership for this activity. In Bali, however, the applicable risk classification brings it within the permanent provincial moratorium. A founder should therefore read the national investment position and the Bali registration position as separate facts: nationally open does not make this activity registrable as PMA in Bali.
